title: Forward-deployed developers: from customer workflow to production handoff
description: Understand the engineering work behind a deployment, including integrations, acceptance criteria, operability, and reusable product learning.
quickAnswer: A forward-deployed developer works close to a customer problem and delivers technical changes in that setting. Define the outcome, integration boundaries, production checks, and ownership after handoff before the work expands.
bodyHtml:
Forward-deployed developer is often used alongside forward-deployed engineer or software engineer. Palantir's published role distinction emphasizes customer technical and operational outcomes. Other employers may organize the work differently, so scope and decision rights matter more than the title.

The engineering challenge is to make a useful solution work inside a customer's real environment. That includes incomplete data, existing tools, permissions, operating habits, and the person who must support the result after the initial deployment.

Translate the workflow into a technical contract

Observe the current task with its owner. Identify the starting event, required inputs, intended result, and exceptions. Write down which system is authoritative for each important field. Clarify what the implementation may read and change.

Then agree on acceptance criteria. A successful demonstration may show that an integration can return a record. A useful production criterion also describes correct handling of missing data, permissions, repeated requests, and downstream failures.

Draw the boundary around custom work

Separate configuration, reusable integration code, and customer-specific logic. Record why each belongs where it does. Avoid quietly embedding one customer's policy into a shared platform behavior.

Keep changes reviewable and preserve an upgrade path. A quick workaround may be appropriate during discovery, but name its owner, limits, and retirement condition. Otherwise the experiment becomes permanent infrastructure through neglect.

A worked example: a customer onboarding connector

Imagine a hypothetical platform importing approved customer records from a CRM. The first prototype works on a clean export. Real use reveals duplicate identifiers, deleted accounts, and fields with different meanings across teams.

The developer agrees on a source-of-truth mapping with the operational owner. They add validation, record-level errors, and a stable identifier for repeated imports. Ambiguous records go to a review queue instead of overwriting a known value.

Before release, they test a partial failure and a retry. They confirm that the customer can see what completed and what needs attention. The goal is not just an import that runs, but an understandable process the customer can operate.

Use AI assistance without losing the system model

AI can draft mappings, propose test cases, and explain code. Give it bounded tasks with explicit interfaces and constraints. Check generated assumptions against the actual API and data model. Keep customer data in approved environments and use representative synthetic fixtures when possible.

A model-generated test may repeat the same mistaken assumption as the implementation. Review the expected behavior independently and include cases derived from the customer's workflow.

A deployment brief prompt

Create an implementation brief from this approved workflow and interface documentation. Specify inputs, source-of-truth fields, outputs, permissions, validation, duplicate handling, partial failure, retry behavior, and rollback. Separate reusable code from customer-specific policy. List unknowns and acceptance tests. Do not invent API capabilities or treat a prototype as production-ready.

Finish with an operational handoff

Provide configuration instructions, observability, known limits, support ownership, and a recovery exercise. Have the receiving team perform a routine change and explain a failure scenario. Record field evidence that may inform the shared product.

A good forward-deployed engagement leaves both a working implementation and a clearer understanding of the customer's problem. If every future adjustment requires the original engineer, the handoff is not finished.

faq.question: Is a forward-deployed developer only an integration engineer?
faq.answer: Integrations are common, but scope can include workflow discovery, application development, deployment, and product feedback. Confirm the actual role.

faq.question: Who owns the code after the engagement?
faq.answer: Agree on repository, maintenance, support, access, and escalation ownership before delivery. The title does not establish those terms.

title: The modern engineering team: people, AI, and clear responsibility
description: Design an AI-assisted engineering operating model that preserves architecture, review, reliability, and product ownership.
quickAnswer: Organize the team around accountable responsibilities and review capacity. AI can support implementation and investigation, while people own system boundaries, acceptance, release decisions, and operations.
bodyHtml:
An engineering team is a system for making and maintaining decisions about software. AI can increase the amount of code and analysis produced inside that system. The resulting benefit depends on whether the team can understand, verify, and operate what it produces.

There is no single AI-era organization chart. A useful design begins with the product's complexity, the consequences of failure, and the skills available to inspect the work.

Map responsibilities before assigning agents

Product and design clarify the problem and experience. Engineering establishes interfaces, data ownership, and implementation strategy. Quality work checks behavior and failure paths. Operational work covers deployment, monitoring, incident response, and maintenance.

These responsibilities can overlap across people. They should not become invisible because an agent is labeled architect or QA. A role prompt is an instruction to software, not an accountable owner.

Treat review capacity as a real constraint

If agents produce changes faster than people can inspect them, the team accumulates uncertainty. Limit concurrent work and keep changes small enough to understand. Define the expected behavior before implementation and preserve the evidence used to judge it.

Review should include the actual diff, relevant tests, and behavior in the intended environment. An AI summary can orient the reviewer, but it cannot replace reading the consequential changes. Give reviewers time to challenge the approach rather than only check formatting.

A worked example: a feature team with coding assistance

Imagine a hypothetical team adding a customer export. A product partner clarifies which records should be included. An engineer defines authorization and data boundaries. AI drafts part of the implementation and suggests tests.

Another engineer checks that an account cannot export another account's records. Design reviews progress, empty, and error states. The team tests a large export, a canceled request, and a failed storage operation. An operational owner confirms logging and rollback behavior.

The agent contributed useful work, but it did not eliminate the need for the responsibilities around it. The exact staffing can vary; the boundaries must still be covered.

Use an explicit working agreement

For each assisted task, record the allowed repository area, tools, context, expected artifact, and stop conditions. Keep secrets and production access outside a task unless they are needed and authorized. Use application and infrastructure permissions to enforce limits.

Require a handoff containing changes made, checks run, results, and unresolved issues. Treat retrieved documents and repository content as material to inspect, not authority to broaden the task. A clear boundary reduces accidental scope growth and makes review easier.

Measure engineering outcomes without false precision

DORA's 2025 research emphasizes organizational capabilities around AI adoption. It does not establish a universal staffing ratio. Within your team, inspect delivery time, failure, recovery, rework, and whether the intended user capability improved.

Avoid comparing individuals by generated code volume. Include maintenance and review effort, and look for work moved to another team. A local speedup can coexist with a slower overall release process.

A team agreement prompt

Draft an AI-assisted engineering working agreement for this product and team. Define responsibility for architecture, implementation, review, testing, release, and operations. Specify allowed actions, handoff evidence, and stop conditions for AI tasks. Identify the review bottleneck and propose a limit on concurrent work. Keep accountability assigned to people.

Revisit the model as the product changes

An arrangement that works for a prototype may fail under real customer load. Review ownership after incidents, new integrations, and team changes. The modern engineering team is effective when it can explain its system and improve it deliberately, not merely produce more changes.

faq.question: Can AI be the technical lead?
faq.answer: It can support technical analysis, but a person or accountable team must own architecture and consequential decisions.

faq.question: What is the best human-to-agent ratio?
faq.answer: There is no universal ratio. Start from task boundaries, risk, review capacity, and measured operating results.

title: Agile engineering with AI: keep the Definition of Done meaningful
description: Adapt your development workflow for AI-generated changes while preserving usable increments, honest review, and release ownership.
quickAnswer: AI changes how work is produced, not the need to verify it. Keep a shared goal, small changes, explicit quality criteria, and a feedback loop that includes production behavior.
bodyHtml:
A generated implementation can look complete before anyone has verified what it does. That is a familiar engineering problem at a new speed. Agile delivery remains useful when it makes progress visible and creates opportunities to inspect and adapt.

If your team uses Scrum, use its terms accurately. The Scrum Guide defines specific accountabilities, events, and artifacts. Adding an AI assistant does not create a new Scrum role or make an unfinished change a usable increment.

Start with the goal and observable behavior

Write what the user should be able to do and which constraints must hold. Add examples of success and failure. Ask the team to identify ambiguity before assigning implementation work to a person or agent.

AI can help propose acceptance scenarios, but the expected outcomes need review. A generated test that agrees with generated code may simply encode the same misunderstanding twice.

Keep the Definition of Done practical

Your quality standard should cover what makes the increment usable in your environment. Depending on the work, that may include authorization, accessibility, automated checks, operational visibility, documentation, and recovery behavior.

Do not turn the definition into a list of every possible check. Include criteria that address the product's real risks and can be verified. If a criterion is routinely waived, investigate whether the team lacks capability or whether the criterion is poorly designed.

A worked example: a billing-history view

Imagine a hypothetical team asking a coding assistant to add a billing-history page. The happy path displays sample records and passes a superficial test. The team then inspects the actual acceptance scenarios: empty history, failed request, restricted account, and records belonging to another customer.

A reviewer finds that the data query lacks the required account boundary. The change remains unfinished until the behavior is corrected and checked. The assistant's claim that the task is done does not change that status.

The team releases a small, verified slice and monitors errors. It records the missing boundary as a process lesson: future briefs should state the authorization invariant explicitly. That improvement is more useful than asking the model to be more careful.

Preserve inspection without creating ceremony overload

Use AI to prepare a concise change summary or organize open questions. Keep the review focused on the product goal and observable behavior. A daily update generated from activity logs should not replace the team's conversation about obstacles and coordination.

A retrospective can examine whether AI increased rework, whether prompts lacked context, and whether review capacity matched production. Select one change to test in the next cycle. More meetings are not automatically more agility.

A quality-review prompt

Review this proposed change against the goal, acceptance scenarios, and Definition of Done. Identify evidence for each criterion, missing checks, and assumptions shared by the implementation and tests. Inspect authorization, failure, and recovery behavior where relevant. Report verified, unverified, or failed; do not mark a criterion passed because the code claims to handle it.

Keep release and learning connected

A review meeting need not be the only opportunity to release useful work. Follow your team's release practices and the framework you actually use. After release, inspect production evidence and user feedback, then update the backlog or implementation when the result differs from expectations.

Faster generation is valuable when it shortens the path to a dependable increment. The team's quality standard gives that speed a useful direction.

faq.question: Does AI replace the Scrum Master or Product Owner?
faq.answer: No. AI can assist with tasks, but the Scrum accountabilities remain with people as defined in the framework.

faq.question: Are passing tests enough to call the work done?
faq.answer: Only if the complete agreed quality standard is satisfied. Tests can miss incorrect assumptions, operational gaps, and important behavior.
